shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Poland's GDP per capita, PPP, as % of Lithuania's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Ninety-eight percent. {p} That's how rich the average Pole is, compared with the average Lithuanian, this year: income per person, adjusted for prices. Both are around sixty thousand dollars, but Lithuania is ahead by about twelve hundred. {pp} In 1995, it was the other way around: the average Pole was almost a fifth richer than the average Lithuanian. Then Lithuania passed Poland in 2003. Poland took the lead back in 2009. And Lithuania passed it again in 2011, and has stayed ahead ever since. {p} And here's the strange part: in the IMF's forecast, the gap stops closing. It's still about twelve hundred dollars in 2031.

In this series, we've measured Poland against Germany: seventy-six percent. Against Czechia: ninety-four. Lithuania is the closest race of all, and the weirdest. {p} It's a country of under three million people, next to a country of thirty-six million. Both joined the European Union on the same day in 2004. And since 1995, both economies have roughly tripled in size. {pp} <soft>So why is the average Lithuanian ahead? Here's the crash that changed everything, the people who left, and why the IMF thinks Poland gets stuck just below a hundred percent.</soft>
Quick one before the chart: this is a series, and the next episode is Britain, the country hundreds of thousands of Poles moved to. Subscribe so you don't miss it. {p} Now, the race.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Poland's GDP per capita, PPP, as % of Lithuania's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Start in 1995. The average Lithuanian produced about seven thousand dollars a year, adjusted for prices. The average Pole, about eight thousand four hundred. {p} Lithuania had a rough start: it broke away from the Soviet Union in 1990, and the Russian financial crisis of 1998 pushed it back into recession in 1999. {p} Then Lithuania took off. Real growth above six percent every single year from 2001 to 2007, and eleven percent in 2007 alone. By 2007, the average Lithuanian was about eighteen percent richer than the average Pole: about three thousand four hundred dollars ahead. {pp} On this chart, that's Poland's line falling far below the dotted line. It looked like Poland would never catch up. And then came 2009.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth, Lithuania (annual %); 2026 is an IMF estimate
shots.narration: Here's Lithuania's economy, year by year, after inflation. {p} 2009: minus fourteen and a half percent. One of the deepest crashes anywhere in the world that year. Poland, as we saw last episode, grew two point six. {pp} So for two years, 2009 and 2010, Poland was ahead again. Lithuanian unemployment hit almost eighteen percent in 2010. {p} And Lithuania chose the hard way out. Its currency was pegged to the euro, so instead of devaluing, it cut wages and public spending.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · PPPPC gap in US$, real GDP growth (NGDP_RPCH)
shots.title: Back on top, and the same growth
shots.narration: It worked, in its own way. Lithuania grew more than six percent in 2011 and passed Poland again that year. It joined the euro in 2015, and by 2021 the average Lithuanian was almost four thousand eight hundred dollars ahead. Since then, the gap has shrunk every single year. {pp} But look at the totals. Since 1995, Lithuania's economy has grown about three point two times, after inflation. Poland's, about three point one times. Almost exactly the same. {p} So where did the gap per person come from? From people.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · population (LP), millions
shots.title: Where everyone went
shots.narration: In 1995, Lithuania had about three point six million people. By 2021, two point eight million. It lost more than a fifth of its population, mostly to emigration: to Britain, Ireland and Norway. When Lithuania joined the EU in 2004, Britain and Ireland opened their job markets to its workers straight away, and wages there were several times higher. After the 2009 crash, another big wave left. {p} Poland lost people too, but far fewer: from thirty-eight and a half million to about thirty-six, around six percent. {pp} The same growth, divided between fewer people, means more income per person. That's a big part of how Lithuania pulled ahead. It's not a happy way to get richer per person, but it shows up in the numbers. {p} And now it's reversing. Since 2021, Lithuania's population has been growing again, to about two point nine million this year, with Lithuanians coming home and people arriving from Ukraine and Belarus.
Now, the scoreboard. {p} And if you're enjoying the series, the subscribe button is right there. Britain is next.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · unemployment rate (% of labor force), 2026 estimate
shots.title: Unemployment, 2026
shots.narration: On jobs, Poland wins easily. Unemployment this year: about three point two percent in Poland, {pp} six point eight in Lithuania. More than double. And Lithuania's rate has been higher than Poland's every year since 2009.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · gross debt (GGXWDG_NGDP), GDP per capita in current US$ (NGDPDPC), inflation (PCPIPCH)
shots.title: Where Lithuania wins, and 2022
shots.narration: Lithuania wins on two others. Government debt: about forty-five percent of the economy, against Poland's sixty-seven. And in plain dollars, without adjusting for prices, the average Lithuanian produces about thirty-six thousand this year, and the average Pole about thirty-one thousand. {p} One more, from 2022, the year energy prices exploded. Inflation hit about nineteen percent in Lithuania, and fourteen in Poland. With the euro, Lithuania couldn't set its own interest rates. Poland could.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Poland's GDP per capita, PPP, as % of Lithuania's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: So, does Poland pass Lithuania again? {p} At the pace of the last ten years, when Poland gained almost one percent a year on Lithuania, it would happen around 2029. {p} But the IMF doesn't see it. In its forecast, Poland gets to about ninety-nine percent of Lithuania next year, and then slips back a little: ninety-eight percent in 2031, still about twelve hundred dollars behind. Both economies grow about two and a half percent a year, so the line just goes flat. {pp} For Poland to pass, one of two things has to happen: Poland grows faster than the IMF expects, or Lithuania's income per person grows slower. And the second one might already be starting. {p} So it's 2029, or not by 2031 at all.

And here's the twist. The thing that made Lithuania richer per person, people leaving, is exactly what it's now trying to reverse. When more people move in, income per person grows more slowly, even if the economy grows faster. {p} So the best outcome for Lithuania might also be the one that lets Poland catch up: a Lithuania that people move to, instead of leave.

<soft>So, your guess: does Poland pass Lithuania again, and when?</soft> Tell me in the comments. {p} If you're watching from Lithuania: did you, or someone in your family, ever work abroad? {p} If you're in Poland: did you expect Lithuania to be ahead? {p} And if you're in Britain: you're next. I read every comment.
And if you missed it, Poland versus Czechia is the next closest race: ninety-four percent, and a date that could be 2030. That story is right here. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Lithuania Passed Poland. Twice.
yt.description:
Income per person, adjusted for prices (IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026): in 1995 the average Pole was almost a fifth richer than the average Lithuanian. Lithuania passed Poland in 2003, lost the lead in the 2009 crash (−14.5%), passed it again in 2011 and is about $1,200 ahead this year (Poland = 98%). Both economies roughly tripled since 1995; Lithuania lost more than a fifth of its people. Who wins on jobs, debt, plain dollars and inflation, and why the IMF's forecast has Poland stuck just below 100% through 2031 (~2029 at the 2016–2026 pace).

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 (PPPPC, NGDPDPC, NGDP_RPCH, LP, LUR, GGXWDG_NGDP, PCPIPCH). The 2029 date is an extrapolation, not an IMF forecast.
